question: When viewed as matrices, which flags of African nations have the same linear algebraic rank as the flag of Denmark? Assume that values in each matrix are chosen so that the rank of each flag is maximal.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the African flags with the same maximal linear-algebraic rank as Denmark are **Benin, Guinea-Bissau, and Madagascar**.

Denmark’s flag, after extending its white cross lines, gives a matrix pattern like  
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R & W & R\\
W & W & W\\
R & W & R
\end{pmatrix},
\]
which has maximal rank \(2\). The relevant African flags are the ones whose stripe layouts reduce to the same two-independent-row/column structure: one full-height vertical band plus a two-color horizontal split on the remaining side. Benin gives essentially  
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
G & Y\\
G & R
\end{pmatrix},
\]
and Madagascar gives  
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
W & R\\
W & G
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Guinea-Bissau has the same underlying structure, with a red full-height band and yellow/green horizontal division; its central star is a single ornament inside the red band and does not add an independent row or column to the maximal rank. Thus these three have maximal rank \(2\), matching Denmark.

Denmark’s flag has a Nordic cross, so in a maximal-rank matrix encoding it gives two independent row/column patterns—essentially a rank-2 matrix. The African flags that match this are those whose color-block matrix also reduces to rank 2. Benin and Madagascar do this because they have a full-height hoist stripe plus two horizontal bands on the fly, giving row patterns like \((s,a,a,\dots)\) and \((s,b,b,\dots)\), which span a 2-dimensional row space.

Guinea-Bissau should be included as well: it has the same red hoist stripe plus yellow/green horizontal bands, and the black star is confined within the red hoist stripe. Since that star does not create a new independent row/column pattern beyond the stripe and horizontal-band split, its maximal rank remains 2, matching Denmark. Thus the matching set is Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree Benin and Madagascar are uncontroversial rank \(2\). The remaining issue is Guinea-Bissau, and I think the exclusion depends on an inconsistent refinement of the matrix.

If we use the same coarse \(3\times 3\) block convention that many of us use for Denmark, Guinea-Bissau can be represented as
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&Y&Y\\
B&Y&Y\\
R&G&G
\end{pmatrix},
\]
which explicitly includes the black star as \(B\), not ignored. Its second and third columns are identical, so its rank is at most \(2\); with distinct \(R,B,Y,G\), it is generically exactly \(2\).

The rank-\(3\) matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&R&Y\\
R&B&Y\\
R&R&G
\end{pmatrix}
\]
only appears if we split the red hoist stripe into left-red / star / right-red columns. That is a finer partition than the coarse \(3\times3\) block convention. If we allow that kind of subdivision for Guinea-Bissau, then we need a clear resolution rule applied to every flag; otherwise the answer becomes resolution-dependent. The problem says values in each matrix are chosen to maximize rank, not that we may keep refining the matrix until the rank increases.

This also separates Guinea-Bissau from Liberia, CAR, and Togo: those have cantons, central bands, or emblems that affect the major full-height/full-width block structure even coarsely. Guinea-Bissau’s star is contained inside the existing full-height hoist stripe and does not create a new full-height column class.

So under the same structural convention that makes Denmark rank \(2\), the consistent set is **Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau**.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I still favor **Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau**, but I want to sharpen the point about the word “maximal.”

The instruction says values in each matrix are chosen so the rank is maximal. It does **not** say we may choose an arbitrarily fine discretization of the flag into matrix cells. If we allow that, the problem becomes resolution-dependent: a curved star can be sampled differently, and the same flag could be rank 2 or rank 3 depending on how many pixels or subdivisions we invent. The Denmark benchmark suggests the intended convention is the flag’s major rectangular color-block structure, not a bitmap scanline model.

Under that block-region convention, Guinea-Bissau has the same L-shaped structure as Benin and Madagascar:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}R&Y\\ R&G\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The black star is contained entirely inside the red hoist block. To get the proposed \(3\times3\) determinant, one must split that single hoist block into red–black–red columns around the star. That is a local refinement, not a new full-height/full-width block division. A matrix with only the hoist column and the fly column has rank at most 2, and with distinct block values it has maximal rank exactly 2.

This also gives a principled distinction from Liberia, Togo, CAR, etc.: those flags have cantons or central stripe structures that break the main full-height/full-width partition even without their emblems. Guinea-Bissau’s star does not create a new hoist/fly division; it is an internal detail inside the hoist stripe. If we exclude Guinea-Bissau solely because it has a star, while treating Denmark’s cross as a coarse block feature, we are not applying the same block-region convention.

So I would not yet drop Guinea-Bissau. Under the natural block-matrix reading, “maximal rank” means choosing distinct values for the distinct blocks so the L-shape determinant is nonzero. That still gives rank 2. The consistent set remains **Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau**.

12.text:
**Current position: Benin and Madagascar only.**

I agree with the majority that the BMG argument relies on an unstated coarse-graining convention. The problem says to choose values so the rank is **maximal**; it does not say to merge away distinct color regions such as Guinea-Bissau’s black star.

Denmark has maximal rank \(2\), and Benin/Madagascar match cleanly:
\[
\text{Benin: }\begin{pmatrix}G&Y\\G&R\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\text{Madagascar: }\begin{pmatrix}W&R\\W&G\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For Guinea-Bissau, the proposed two-column matrix
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&Y\\
B&Y\\
B&G\\
R&G
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is not a faithful matrix of the flag: it collapses the entire red hoist stripe into one black cell in star rows. But the actual rows through the star have a red–black–red pattern inside the hoist stripe, not a single black value. Once that is represented, a submatrix like
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&R&R&Y\\
R&B&R&Y\\
R&R&R&G
\end{pmatrix}
\]
already has rank at least \(3\) for generic distinct \(R,B,Y,G\), since the second row differs from the first only in the star column, while the third row differs from the first only in the fly color.

So under the literal maximal-rank interpretation, Guinea-Bissau’s star cannot be ignored or absorbed. The consistent set remains:

\[
\boxed{\text{Benin and Madagascar only}}
\]

If the group wants to adopt a coarse block-region convention that deliberately ignores non-rectangular emblems, that must be stated explicitly and applied uniformly; otherwise it conflicts with the “maximal rank” instruction.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I still favor **Benin, Madagascar, and Guinea-Bissau** as the consistent set.

The strongest objection is that “maximal rank” forces the black star to count, because a refined matrix such as
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&R&Y\\
R&B&Y\\
R&R&G
\end{pmatrix}
\]
has rank 3 for generic distinct colors. But that objection already assumes we are allowed to subdivide the red hoist stripe horizontally so that the star gets its own column. That is not what the problem says. It says the *values in each matrix* are chosen so rank is maximal; it does not say we may replace one flag’s natural block matrix with a finer matrix only for Guinea-Bissau.

Under the same block-region convention that makes Denmark rank 2, Guinea-Bissau is an L-shaped flag: one full-height hoist stripe, plus a two-band fly field. Its star is contained inside the hoist stripe and does not create a new full-height column class or full-width row class. A coarse encoding such as
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
R&Y\\
B&Y\\
B&G\\
R&G
\end{pmatrix}
\]
has only two column classes, hence rank at most 2, and generically exactly 2.
